references.text: Joseph's interpretation of Pharaoh's dream: seven good years followed by seven years of severe famine that will consume the land – the situation verse 36 prepares for.
Joseph proposes appointing overseers to collect one-fifth of the harvests during the good years – the plan of which verse 36 is a part.
Implementation of the plan: during the seven good years, Joseph gathered enormous amounts of grain in the cities, as a direct fulfillment of verse 36.
When the famine came, Joseph opened the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians and people from other lands – the stored food prevented the land from perishing, just as verse 36 predicted.
Joseph explains to his brothers that the famine has lasted two years with five more to come, and that God sent him to preserve life – a confirmation of the necessity of storing food.
The famine was very severe in Egypt and Canaan, and the people came to Joseph for food – emphasizing the seriousness that the preparations in verse 36 accounted for.
The ant gathers food during summer and autumn as preparation – a principle of wisdom that mirrors Joseph's plan to store food in good years to survive the bad ones.
The verses form connected parts of the same prophecy and action plan: the warning about hunger (v.30) is the direct cause of the call to make provisions (v.36).
The verse shows the practical fulfillment of the strategic plan described in the source verse; the storage (v.48) is the answer to the need to save the land from hunger (v.36).
The verse confirms that the seven years of famine occurred as predicted, demonstrating the effectiveness of the storage mandated in the source verse.
The verse describes the first phase (abundance), which is absolutely necessary to carry out the storage required by the source verse.
A clear thematic parallel: both verses describe God's command to store food as a rescue plan to preserve life during an impending global catastrophe (the flood versus the famine).
